title: Reading Jonah

objectives.can: Read Jonah 1 continuously with only occasional help.

explanation.summary: Jonah is a short book that tells one story in plain prose, and a good book to read whole. Its first chapter is built from a few repeated words, and the sailors' speech gives you a great deal of everyday Hebrew. This lesson reads Jonah 1:1–10.

sections.heading: What you will meet in Jonah
body: Jonah is a prophetic book that is told as a story. It begins like the prophetic books, with the word of the LORD coming to a prophet, but then it is narrative from beginning to end, with wayyiqtol chains, short speeches and a few songs and prayers. Its vocabulary is small and repeated, and its sentences are short.

The passage for this lesson is Jonah 1:1–10. The rest of the first chapter is 1:11–16: the sailors ask what to do, Jonah tells them to throw him into the sea, they try to row back, they pray and cast him in, the storm stops, and they fear the LORD and offer sacrifice.

sections.heading: The word of the LORD and the command
body: The opening, וַיְהִי דְּבַר יְהוָה אֶל יוֹנָה בֶן אֲמִתַּי לֵאמֹר, is the usual way for a prophetic book to introduce the word of the LORD. The verb וַיְהִי is singular because its subject is the construct chain דְּבַר יְהוָה, 'the word of the LORD'. The infinitive לֵאמֹר leads into the speech.

The speech in 1:2 is three imperatives: קוּם, לֵךְ, and וּקְרָא. The first two are the pair 'get up, go' that you have met in earlier readings. The reason is given by כִּי and a qatal, עָלְתָה רָעָתָם לְפָנָי, 'their evil has come up before me'. Everything that follows in the story tests what Jonah does with these commands.

sections.heading: Repeated words
body: A reader of Jonah soon notices that a few words keep coming back. The adjective גָּדוֹל, 'great', is used for the city (הָעִיר הַגְּדוֹלָה, 1:2), for the wind (רוּחַ גְּדוֹלָה, 1:4), for the storm (סַעַר גָּדוֹל, 1:4), and for the sailors' fear (1:10). Each time the adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun it follows, so it is a good place to practise agreement.

The verb קוּם, 'rise', is the first command of 1:2. In 1:3 Jonah does rise (וַיָּקָם), but only to flee. In 1:6 the captain says קוּם to him again. The verb יָרַד, 'go down', is another thread: in 1:3 Jonah goes down to Joppa and goes down into the ship (וַיֵּרֶד twice), and in 1:5 he has gone down further, into the hold of the ship (יָרַד). The story goes down step by step, and the commands go up.
The sea and the ship also come back, and the verb of throwing, הֵטִיל in 1:4 and וַיָּטִלוּ in 1:5: the LORD hurls a wind, and the sailors hurl the cargo.

sections.heading: A cognate object and a surprising subject
body: Jonah 1:10 says וַיִּירְאוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים יִרְאָה גְדוֹלָה. The verb וַיִּירְאוּ and the noun יִרְאָה come from the same root, and the noun, with the adjective, is the object. This is a cognate object: the noun repeats the idea of the verb and the adjective adds the size, 'they feared a great fear', that is, they were very afraid. The same words begin the end of the chapter, in 1:16, with the object אֶת יְהוָה added.

In 1:4 the surprise is the subject. The ship is the subject of חִשְּׁבָה לְהִשָּׁבֵר, literally 'the ship thought to be broken'. A feminine singular verb, a feminine noun וְהָאֳנִיָּה, and then an infinitive: the ship is spoken of as if it could think, and the clause means that it threatened to break up. Such a figure is common in Hebrew narrative.

sections.heading: The sailors' speech
body: The sailors' speech is the largest part of the passage, and it is mostly questions and plans. The captain's words in 1:6 are two imperatives, קוּם and קְרָא, a question מַה לְּךָ נִרְדָּם, and a hope with אוּלַי and a yiqtol, יִתְעַשֵּׁת, 'perhaps he will give thought'. In 1:7 the sailors say לְכוּ, 'come', and two cohortatives, וְנַפִּילָה and וְנֵדְעָה, 'let us cast' and 'let us know'. In 1:8 they ask מַה מְּלַאכְתְּךָ וּמֵאַיִן תָּבוֹא, 'what is your work, and where do you come from', and further questions about the land and the people.

Jonah's answer in 1:9 puts the predicate first in עִבְרִי אָנֹכִי, 'a Hebrew I am', and then sets the object before the verb in וְאֶת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם אֲנִי יָרֵא. Putting the object first draws attention to it: it is the LORD whom he fears. His answer is not a reply to every question, only to the ones that matter to him.

sections.heading: Hard places
body: Jonah has a few unusual words and forms. In 1:7 and again in 1:12 the relative word is the short form שֶׁ, in בְּשֶׁלְּמִי and בְשֶׁלִּי, where the book at other times uses אֲשֶׁר, as in 1:8 בַּאֲשֶׁר לְמִי. Grammarians connect the short form with a later stage of the language, but the book has both. The word יַרְכְּתֵי in 1:5 is a rare noun meaning the far parts of something; in this verse it is the inner part of the ship.

Other difficulties are not grammatical. Tarshish in 1:3 is a far place whose exact location is not certain, and the verse writes the name in two ways, once with the ending ה for to (תַּרְשִׁישָׁה) and once without it (תַרְשִׁישׁ). We read the names as the text has them.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read 1:1–10 straight through. Underline the repeated words, then go through it again and ask of each verb whether it is an event (wayyiqtol), a background clause (subject first, as in 1:5, where Jonah has already gone down) or part of a speech. Look up a word only when you have tried the sentence.

misunderstandings: Thinking that the book is a single poem or a parable because it is short. It is told as a narrative and is read with the same tools as any narrative: wayyiqtol chains, background clauses and speech.
Taking a repeated word as a copying error. The repetition of גָּדוֹל and יָרַד is a deliberate feature of the style.
Reading the cognate object as two separate ideas. The noun repeats the verb and the adjective adds the size: they were very afraid.
Treating the short relative שֶׁ as a mistake. It is a real form, used in Jonah beside אֲשֶׁר.

deeper.heading: Language and date
body: Some scholars use features such as the short relative שֶׁ and the vocabulary to place Jonah late in the history of Hebrew, and others point out that such forms also occur in early texts and in northern speech. The grammar can describe the features, but a reading course does not decide the date of the book.

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: 'Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and proclaim against it; for their wickedness is come up before Me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three imperatives, קוּם, לֵךְ and וּקְרָא, are the command. The adjective הַגְּדוֹלָה follows הָעִיר and agrees with it in gender, number and definiteness. The qatal עָלְתָה with the subject רָעָתָם gives the reason, with the suffix -ָם for 'their'.

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD; and he went down to Joppa, and found a ship going to Tarshish; so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish, from the presence of the LORD.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Jonah does rise, וַיָּקָם, but the infinitive לִבְרֹחַ, 'to flee', says why, and the place is away from the LORD: מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה. Then a chain of wayyiqtol verbs takes him down: וַיֵּרֶד, וַיִּמְצָא, וַיִּתֵּן, וַיֵּרֶד.

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: And the mariners were afraid, and cried every man unto his god; and they cast forth the wares that were in the ship into the sea, to lighten it unto them. But Jonah was gone down into the innermost parts of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The sailors' actions are wayyiqtol: they feared, they cried, they hurled. Then the subject comes first, וְיוֹנָה יָרַד, with a qatal: this is background and contrast, Jonah had gone down to the hold. The next two wayyiqtol verbs, וַיִּשְׁכַּב and וַיֵּרָדַם, return to the line of events.

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: And they said every one to his fellow: 'Come, and let us cast lots, that we may know for whose cause this evil is upon us.' So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Jonah.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The imperative לְכוּ and the two cohortatives וְנַפִּילָה and וְנֵדְעָה are the plan; the relative בְּשֶׁלְּמִי uses the short שֶׁ. The next verbs are wayyiqtol: they cast, the lot fell, and it fell on Jonah.

examples.analysis: A cognate object: the verb וַיִּירְאוּ and the noun יִרְאָה, with the adjective גְדוֹלָה, 'they feared a great fear'. Then the question מַה זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ, 'what is this you have done', with a qatal in the second person.

quoted.english: And he said unto them: 'I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who hath made the sea and the dry land.'

options: It changes the verb into the past tense

It makes the sentence a question
check.explain: The usual order puts the verb first. Putting the object first draws attention to it. This is a tendency of Hebrew word order, and the sense here is that Jonah answers the question of who he is by naming whom he fears.

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: Then were the men exceedingly afraid, and said unto him: 'What is this that thou hast done?' For the men knew that he fled from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.

options: A cognate object: the noun is of the same root as the verb, and the sense is that the men were very afraid
check.explain: The verb and the noun come from the same root. The adjective גְדוֹלָה agrees with the feminine noun יִרְאָה. The whole phrase reports intense fear.

reading.why: The opening of the book in ten verses: the word of the LORD and the commands, the repeated words גָּדוֹל, קוּם and יָרַד, a cognate object, background clauses, and a long stretch of dialogue spoken by the sailors and Jonah.
